bib.title: Researcher Freedom: Good Vibrations? (Chapter 9, Statistics Done Wrong)
bib.venue: book chapter, Statistics Done Wrong (no starred year printed in the chapter)

question: How does the analyst's freedom to choose measures, covariates, exclusions, groupings and stopping rules inflate false positives, and how can it be limited?
hypothesis: Analysis choices made after seeing the data bias results and inflate false-positive rates even without intent; fixing the analysis beforehand reduces this.

results.claim: One scientific hypothesis maps to many statistical hypotheses, so accepting any of several outcomes as support inflates false positives.
results.setup: Argument with examples (a dozen side effects, red/pink/other clothing).

results.claim: The choice of analysis is always data-dependent, so uncertainty estimates (standard errors, confidence intervals) are biased and false positives inflated.
results.quote:
But the choice of analysis strategy is always based on the
data.

limits: No data of its own; every quantitative claim is quoted from footnoted work and the footnote list is not in the extracted text.
Prespecification is not always possible or right: assumptions about distributions and outliers can be wrong, and some data (market crash, cancer patients) cannot be replicated.
Blinding techniques for common statistical methods need further methodological research; triple blinding does not remove all bias.
practices: Plan the data analysis before collecting data, accounting for multiple comparisons and listing the effects to look for (Tips, p.95).
Register the clinical trial protocol where applicable (Tips, p.95).
If you deviate from the protocol, say so in the paper and explain why (Tips, p.95).
Have a specific statistical hypothesis in mind before analysing; do not torture the data (Tips, p.95).
Use blind analysis: hide the value of interest, add a hidden constant, split analysis across independent groups, or inject then remove false data (p.94).
Replicate prepublication on a new independent dataset with the same methods and adequate power when possible (p.95).
When the plan proves wrong, correct the analysis and disclose it rather than run an obviously wrong preplanned one (p.95).
Consider protocol registration for confirmatory research in psychology and similar fields (p.95).
